teaser: Two years, some sixty studies and a wall-sized canvas, all to paint a lazy afternoon.

lesson.text: This canvas is about 2 meters high and 3 meters wide, roughly 7 by 10 feet. Stand in front of it in Chicago and the nearest figures are almost your own height. Georges Seurat was 24 when he started it, and he covered that whole surface with strokes no bigger than a grain of rice.

The place is real. La Grande Jatte is a long island in the Seine, just west of Paris. In the 1880s, people of every class took the ferry there on Sundays to stroll, row, fish and flirt. Seurat went again and again with a small wooden panel and a box of paints.

He did not paint the big picture outdoors, though. He made around sixty studies, small oil sketches and soft black crayon drawings, then built the final scene in his studio like an architect assembling a facade. Each figure was tried out, moved, enlarged or dropped.

lesson.title: Who came to the island
lesson.text: About fifty people share this lawn. Meet a few of them, from the front of the stage to the back.

spots.title: The fashionable couple
spots.text: Top hat, cane, and a skirt puffed out by a bustle, a padded frame worn at the back. They are the tallest figures and the most rigid, cut out like paper silhouettes.

spots.title: Three strangers
spots.text: A rower in a sleeveless shirt smokes a pipe. Behind him sit a woman sewing and a gentleman in a top hat. Three social worlds on one patch of grass, and nobody speaks.

spots.title: Horn and soldiers
spots.text: A man blows a brass horn toward the river. Just to his right, two soldiers stand at attention like tin toys. Seurat keeps even the noise of the park perfectly still.

spots.title: The girl in white
spots.text: Almost everyone here is seen in profile or from behind. This child, dressed in white, is the one figure who faces you straight on, right at the heart of the canvas.

lesson.text: Did you feel how quiet it is? A park full of people, dogs and music should be noisy. Seurat admired ancient Egyptian and Greek friezes, the long carved bands of figures on temples, and he wanted modern Parisians to walk with the same solemn dignity.
Seurat disliked the word “pointillism”, which critics used half mockingly. He preferred “divisionism” or the grander “chromo-luminarism”, meaning painting with color and light.

Now, the famous dots. Seurat had read scientists such as the chemist Chevreul, who showed that two colors placed side by side change each other. Put orange next to blue and both look stronger. So instead of stirring colors together on the palette, he set small touches of pure color next to one another and let your eye do the blending from a distance.

lesson.title: What the grass is made of
lesson.text: From far away, the lawn is green and the shadows are dark green. Move closer and that stops being true.

spots.title: Sunlit grass
spots.text: Yellow, light green and specks of orange. The orange is the warmth of the sun itself, sprinkled over the lawn.

spots.title: Shaded grass
spots.text: The shadow is not just darker. It holds blue and violet touches, the cool opposites of sunlight, mixed among deep greens.

spots.title: The dark skirt
spots.text: Nothing here is flat black. The dress is woven from blues, violets and reds, which is why it seems to glow instead of forming a hole in the picture.

lesson.text: Seurat's idea: color is not mixed in the paint, it is mixed in your eye. Small touches of pure color, placed side by side, fuse when you step back.

The dots came late. Seurat first painted the scene with ordinary crisscrossed strokes in 1884 and 1885. Then, convinced by his reading, he went back over the entire canvas with tiny touches. That second campaign is why the surface seems to shimmer.

Under the shimmer sits a very strict skeleton. Every figure stands upright or lies flat, and the island itself slides away in one long slant. Trace that scaffolding and you will see why nothing in this crowd seems able to move.
Three kinds of line hold fifty people in place.

lines.label: The shore
lines.text: The riverbank cuts the picture on a long diagonal. It pulls your eye from the reclining rower at lower left to the tiny strollers far away.

lines.label: The couple's vertical
lines.text: The couple at right stands like a column from top hat to hem. It is the tallest upright in the picture and anchors the whole right side.

lines.label: The central axis
lines.text: The woman under the red parasol and the girl in white mark the middle of the canvas. The rest of the crowd is arranged around this quiet pair.

lines.label: The far bank
lines.text: A flat horizontal closes the distance. Verticals, a horizontal, one diagonal: the scene is built like a stage set.

lesson.text: With the structure in mind, the oddities stand out more. Seurat slipped a few strange guests into this orderly Sunday, and Parisians of 1886 noticed them at once.
One visitor has brought a pet that is definitely not a dog. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The monkey
spots.text: A small monkey on a leash, tail curled, beside the lady's skirt. Pet monkeys were a fashionable luxury. Some historians also read it as a sly hint about its owner's morals, but nobody knows.

lesson.text: The same doubt hangs over the woman fishing at the far left edge. In French, the verbs for “to fish” and “to sin” sound almost alike, and some writers think Seurat was making a joke about women looking for clients. He never explained. He let the stiff silhouettes keep their secrets.

One of Seurat's modern pigments betrayed him. The zinc yellow he mixed into the sunlit grass began turning a dull brownish ochre within a few years, so the lawn you see is less bright than the one he painted.

The picture was shown in May 1886 at the eighth and last Impressionist exhibition. Many visitors laughed at the wooden figures. But the young critic Félix Fénéon saw something new and gave it a name: Neo-Impressionism. Impressionists caught a fleeting moment by instinct. Seurat wanted to rebuild it with method.

He was not quite finished with it. A couple of years later he painted a border of colored dots all around the image, changing its tints to contrast with whatever part of the scene it touches. You can still see that speckled band at the edges.

spots.title: The painted border
spots.text: Reds, blues and oranges in tiny dots. Seurat added this band later so that the picture would carry its own transition to the frame.

spots.title: The woman fishing
spots.text: She holds a rod over the Seine in her Sunday dress. Whether she is simply fishing or part of a pun, Seurat left open.

spots.title: The black dog
spots.text: A big dog sniffs the remains of a picnic. Its curved back and tail are among the few supple lines in a picture of stiff uprights.

spots.title: The little dog
spots.text: A small dog with a ribbon leaps toward the black one. It is the liveliest creature on the island.

spots.title: Sails on the Seine
spots.text: White sails, a rowing boat, a steam launch. The river was as crowded as the lawn on Sundays.

spots.title: The running girl
spots.text: A child in orange dashes across the sunlit grass, one of the rare figures caught in motion.

spots.title: The red parasol
spots.text: A warm orange-red dome against cool green leaves. Opposite colors side by side make each other look brighter, the rule behind the whole picture.

lesson.text: In 1924 the Chicago collector Frederic Clay Bartlett bought the painting for about 20,000 dollars. Two years later he gave it to the Art Institute of Chicago, where it has become the museum's best-known picture.

It almost did not survive a trip. In 1958 the painting was on loan to the Museum of Modern Art in New York when a fire broke out in the building. It was carried out unharmed, and Chicago has never lent it since. To see those seven by ten feet of dots, you have to go to them.

quiz.question: Roughly how big is the painting?
options: About the size of a book
quiz.explanation: It measures roughly 2 by 3 meters, or 7 by 10 feet.

quiz.question: Where did Seurat want colors to mix?
quiz.explanation: He placed pure touches side by side so the eye blends them from a distance.

quiz.question: Which figure faces the viewer straight on?
quiz.explanation: The child in white at the center is the one figure seen fully from the front.

quiz.question: What unusual pet appears at the lower right?
quiz.explanation: A small monkey on a leash stands beside the fashionable lady.

quiz.question: What happened to the zinc yellow in the grass?
quiz.explanation: The pigment darkened to a dull ochre within a few years.

quiz.question: Who gave Seurat's new approach the name Neo-Impressionism?
quiz.explanation: Fénéon coined the term after seeing the painting in 1886.

facts.text: Seurat painted the large canvas outdoors on the island in a few Sundays.
facts.explanation: He made about sixty studies on site, then built the picture in his studio over two years.

facts.text: The dotted border around the scene was added by Seurat a couple of years after the first showing.
facts.explanation: He painted the band of colored dots later, to link the image to its frame.
He disliked that word and preferred “divisionism” or “chromo-luminarism”.
